# Columbia Accident Investigation Board, Report Volume I (light reference)

**Source:** Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003). *Report, Volume I*. August 2003. U.S. Government Printing Office; NASA Technical Reports Server record 20030093634. Public domain (US Government work, 17 USC §105; NTRS: "Work of the US Gov. Public Use Permitted."). Third-party material inside it is paraphrased, never quoted: passages the report quotes from outside works (Vaughan, Feynman's appendix to the Rogers report, Turner, Tufte, the Rogers Commission and earlier review boards), the Boeing-credited figure in Chapter 9 and the Boeing slide in Chapter 7, and the words of named individuals in quoted e-mails, logs, transcripts and testimony. The text comes from an OCR layer; quotations are taken only from clean Board prose.
**Structure:** Board Statement, Executive Summary, Synopsis; Part One, the accident (Ch 1 programme history, Ch 2 the final flight, Ch 3 accident analysis, Ch 4 other factors); Part Two, why it occurred (Ch 5 from Challenger to Columbia, Ch 6 decision making, Ch 7 organisational causes, Ch 8 history as cause); Part Three, a look ahead (Ch 9 future of human space flight, Ch 10 other observations, Ch 11 recommendations); Appendices A–C (the investigation, members, staff). 250 pages, read in full; text-only image scope.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The Board finds two causes of equal weight: "We are convinced that the management practices overseeing the Space Shuttle Program were as much a cause of the accident as the foam that struck the left wing." [V] (Synopsis, p. 11). Physically, foam from the left bipod ramp struck the left wing in the vicinity of the lower half of RCC panel 8 at 81.9 seconds and opened a breach through which hot gas entered the wing on re-entry (Executive Summary, p. 9). Organisationally, the causes were rooted in the programme's history and culture: the compromises that won its approval, resource constraints, shifting priorities, schedule pressure, treating a developmental vehicle as operational, and no agreed national vision; and in practices that grew from them, chiefly reliance on past success instead of sound engineering, barriers that blocked safety information and stifled dissent, unintegrated management, and an informal chain of command operating outside the rules (Ch 7, p. 177).

The Board frames itself against investigations that stop at the broken part or the nearest person: "Such corrections lead to a misguided and potentially disastrous belief that the underlying problem has been solved." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). Foam shedding violated design requirements from the first flight and was progressively redefined as acceptable, the pattern the Board, borrowing from Diane Vaughan, calls the normalisation of deviance, and the same pattern preceded Challenger (Ch 6, p. 130; Ch 8, p. 196). "History is not just a backdrop or a scene-setter. History is cause. History set the Columbia and Challenger accidents in motion." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195). Replacing people will not fix it: NASA's problems "cannot be solved simply by retirements, resignations, or transferring personnel." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195).

## The physical cause and its analysis (Ch 1–4)

- **Origins.** The Shuttle was designed under a cost ceiling to be all things to all users, and the Board judges that "the greatest compromise NASA made was not so much with any particular element of the technical design, but rather with the premise of the vehicle itself" [V] (Ch 1, p. 23); it was always "a developmental vehicle that operates not in routine flight but in the realm of dangerous exploration" [V] (Ch 1, p. 25).
- **The foam.** Hand-sprayed bipod foam that could be inspected only visually; "A combination of factors, rather than a single factor, led to the loss of the left bipod foam ramp" [V] (Ch 3, p. 52). The RCC had been specified with essentially no impact resistance and could not be inspected adequately (Ch 3, p. 58).
- **Proof.** The Board's own test, a 1.67-pound foam block at 777 feet per second, opened a hole of about 16 by 17 inches in a flown RCC panel 8, and "counteracted the lingering denial or discounting of the analytic evidence" [V] (Ch 3, pp. 81–83).
- **Mission data were enough.** The information available during the mission was adequate to judge the strike's effect on tile and RCC (Ch 3, p. 62); by the time trouble reached Mission Control's telemetry, the damage was unrecoverable (Ch 3, p. 73).
- **Other factors.** A fault tree of more than 3,000 elements closed out most alternative explanations (Synopsis, p. 12; Ch 4, pp. 85–86), but surfaced lapses in bolt-catcher qualification, two closeout processes that a single person can perform, and a "statistically deceptive" redefinition of foreign-object debris (Ch 4, pp. 86–95).

## Drift: from Challenger to Columbia (Ch 5)

Post-Challenger reforms were partly undone. "By the eve of the Columbia accident, institutional practices that were in effect at the time of the Challenger accident — such as inadequate concern over deviations from expected performance, a silent safety program, and schedule pressure — had returned to NASA." [V] (Ch 5, p. 101). The Shuttle lost about 40 percent of its purchasing power in a decade; its workforce was cut on the assurance that safety would not suffer; a 1995 report called it mature and reliable, a view the Board rejects; and, with NASA committed to a Space Station deadline of 19 February 2004, the White House and Congress had put it "on probation" (Ch 5, pp. 104–117). "The Program was operating too close to too many margins." [V] (Ch 5, p. 118).

## Decision making (Ch 6)

- **Normalising foam.** "With each successful landing, it appears that NASA engineers and managers increasingly regarded the foam-shedding as inevitable, and as either unlikely to jeopardize safety or simply an acceptable risk." [V] (Ch 6, p. 122). After STS-112's bipod loss, the In-Flight Anomaly the photo working group recommended was instead assigned as an "action", and "The Space Shuttle Program decided to fly not one but two missions before resolving the STS-112 foam loss." [V] (Ch 6, p. 125). Its flight rationale "is seriously flawed": "With no engineering analysis, Shuttle managers used past success as a justification for future flights" [V] (Ch 6, p. 126).
- **Schedule pressure.** "The weight of evidence supports the workforce view." [V] that there was pressure to hold the Node 2 date (Ch 6, p. 131); "No one at NASA wants to be the one to stand up and say, "We can't make that date."" [V] (Ch 6, p. 138); most of the Program's concern about Columbia's strike was about the threat to the schedule (Ch 6, p. 139).
- **During the mission.** Three imagery requests were made and turned down, and at least eight opportunities were missed (Ch 6, p. 140). Crater was used far outside its validated range, and "The assumptions and uncertainty embedded in this analysis were never fully presented to the Mission Evaluation Room or the Mission Management Team." [V] (Ch 6, p. 145). The engineers' request, routed through engineering rather than mission channels, was seen as a desire rather than a need (Ch 6, p. 152); they were asked to show a "mandatory" need for the very images that would let them assess the damage (Ch 6, p. 157).
- **The Board's diagnosis.** "The engineers found themselves in the unusual position of having to prove that the situation was unsafe — a reversal of the usual requirement to prove that a situation is safe." [V] "Mission management welcomed this opinion and sought no others." [V] "Managers' tendency to accept opinions that agree with their own dams the flow of effective communications." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169). "Managers' claims that they didn't hear the engineers' concerns were due in part to their not asking or listening." [V] (Ch 6, p. 170). Safety representatives were present but passive (Ch 6, p. 172).
- **Rescue.** A rescue by Atlantis "was considered challenging but feasible" [V] had the damage been understood early (Ch 6, p. 174).

## Organisational causes (Ch 7)

"In the Board's view, NASA's organizational culture and structure had as much to do with this accident as the External Tank foam." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). NASA's safety culture had become "reactive, complacent, and dominated by unjustified optimism" [V], and "At every juncture of STS-107, the Shuttle Program's structure and processes, and therefore the managers in charge, resisted new information." [V] (Ch 7, pp. 180–181). Benchmarks from the Navy's submarine and reactor programmes: airing minority opinions ("when no minority opinions are present, the responsibility for a thorough and critical examination falls to management" [V], Ch 7, p. 183), written technical work instead of slides, and separation of technical authority from cost and schedule (Ch 7, pp. 182–184). Information was rolled up, abbreviated and simplified as it rose through the hierarchy (Ch 7, p. 190). "NASA inverted this burden of proof." [V] (Ch 7, p. 190). "Imagine the difference if any Shuttle manager had simply asked, "Prove to me that Columbia has not been harmed."" [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). Recommendations: an independent Technical Engineering Authority owning requirements and waivers, safety with line authority and its own resources, and a true Integration Office (Ch 7, p. 193).

## History as cause (Ch 8)

The mechanism of normalisation: "For both O-rings and foam, that first decision was a turning point. It established a precedent for accepting, rather than eliminating, these technical deviations." [V]; the experience base "functioned as an elastic waistband, expanding to hold larger deviations from the original design" [V] (Ch 8, p. 196). "Taken one at a time, each decision seemed correct." [V] (Ch 8, p. 197). Systemic statements: conflicting goals of cost, schedule and safety; bureaucratic accountability in place of deference to engineers ("Management did not listen to what their engineers were telling them. Instead, rules and procedures took priority." [V], Ch 8, p. 201); hierarchy that silenced ("Status mattered. In its absence, numbers were the great equalizer." [V], Ch 8, p. 202); dependence on contractors; and a silent safety system (Ch 8, pp. 200–202). Principles for change: "Leaders create culture. It is their responsibility to change it." [V]; "NASA's challenge is to design systems that maximize the clarity of signals, amplify weak signals so they can be tracked, and account for missing signals." [V]; and "NASA's blind spot is it believes it has a strong safety culture." [V] (Ch 8, p. 203).

## A look ahead (Ch 9–11) and the investigation (App A)

Human space flight "must be viewed as a developmental activity" [V] (Ch 9, p. 208); vigilance after an accident "will inevitably dissipate over time" [V] (Ch 9, p. 208), so the organisational changes must be made, and the harder cultural changes need top-level leadership. Chapter 10 records "weak signals" that did not cause the accident (quality-assurance decay at Kennedy, ageing systems, drawings, leadership training), and Chapter 11 lists the recommendations (Ch 10, pp. 213–223; Ch 11, pp. 225–227). Appendix A explains the Board's method: a safety investigation, not one to assign blame; privileged witness statements to obtain full disclosure; and personal accountability left to a separate process, since a safety investigation "does not prevent an accounting of personal responsibility associated with an accident" [V] (App A, p. 233).

## Key Connections

- **Rogers Commission (1986):** the baseline; many of its remedies undone (Ch 5, Ch 8).
- **Diane Vaughan:** normalisation of deviance; also on the Board's staff (Ch 6, p. 130; Ch 8; App C, p. 244).
- **High Reliability and Normal Accident theories; Navy SUBSAFE, Naval Reactors, Aerospace Corporation:** yardsticks and benchmarks (Ch 7, pp. 180–184).
- **Turner, Tufte, Feynman:** failures of foresight; slide analysis; the Russian-roulette comparison, which the Board says is only possible in hindsight (Ch 7, p. 191; Ch 8, pp. 195, 197).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

- An accident with a technical cause still has organisational causes of equal weight; stopping at the part and the person leaves the problem in place (Part Two, p. 97; Ch 7, p. 177).
- Past success is not evidence of safety; operations must be proved safe, not proved unsafe (Ch 6, p. 126; Ch 7, p. 190).
- Anomalies that do not end in disaster should not be read as data that justify the next flight; that reading is how deviance was normalised (Ch 8, p. 196).
- The Shuttle was never operational, and space cannot be explored on a fixed-cost basis (Ch 8, p. 203).
- Leaders own the culture and the conditions for their subordinates' success or failure (Ch 8, p. 203).
